# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code

**seeding**
: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

**base build**
: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.

**old code**
: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.

Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.

## Finding or building a base build

- If your brief names a base build, use it.
- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.

      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
      ant compileAll
      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean

If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.

## Seeding a worktree

A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.

Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.

    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]

- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.

## Running the old code

If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.

`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:

    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM

- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).

To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:

    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss

The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".
# Running tests

**track**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.

**shard**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.

**code state**
: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

## The two suites

`ant testFast` runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:

- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.

`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.

`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.

The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:

    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'

The two suites work in the same way:

- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.

To run a suite:

- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.

## The switches that the harness reads

Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.

- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.

## Outside the gate

- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).

## When to run a whole suite

- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk or of a phase that both paths share, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`) or the parser, run both.
- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the run time (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.

The suites do not check these:

- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
- the linker's aliasing of apis;
- `fortress unparse`;
- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.

If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.

## One test, or a few

Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.

### Interpreter tests

Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]

- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.

To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test

Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

## One unit-test class, or one track

To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.

To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:

- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'

  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;
`remove F-90`; `merge F-91 into F-87`; `note F-87`, or `note F-87 correcting
TIME`, a noted block. Each may be followed by one indented provenance line of
its own:
`  from: PATH, "HEADING"; commit: HASH; by: WHO; note: WHY`. Blank lines and
`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped:
to add to its history, write `note F-87`. A note whose block the history holds
already, all but its time, is skipped too, so a file run twice writes nothing
twice. One call writes one block per entry, so an entry is noted, or changed,
once in a file.

check fails on: an entry line without its number, or a line under an entry
that continues it; a number on two lines; a number with no `numbered` or
`added` block, or one gone from its file whose last block is not `merged into`
or `removed`; a noted block that holds an earlier line, or whose `correcting`
names no earlier block of its entry, or more than one; a pointer to no live
entry, or quoted words that do not open the target's title; with --base, an
entry at COMMIT that is neither its line now nor the earlier line of a block
in its history (pointer words refreshed by the tool aside). It reports, without failing: the entries over 600 characters, the
entries without a bold title, and the `--from` paths and the report sections

# Keeping the record

How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.

**history**
: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.

**pointer**
: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."

**pass**
: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.

## What an entry is

An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.

Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:

1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.

In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:

- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.

An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:

- keep: every check passes;
- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.

Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.

## Reading and writing

- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
- Commit the record file and its history together.
- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.

## The pass

Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.

The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.

1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.

Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.

## A consolidation

A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. Run it on FACTS before each batch launches, since the batch's workers read it.

- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.
add, rewrite, close and duplicate check the whole line they write; note checks
only what it changes (the notes cell and the row's length), so that a row
failing the template elsewhere still takes a note. A row at its length limit
takes no note: rewrite cuts it back (the rework's decision D4, "each is cut
when next edited", process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md).

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored
  add FILE --section TITLE   FILE holds one row line, its # cell `?` (or the
                             seven cells after it); numbers it max + 1 and
                             inserts it in that section's table in number
                             order
  note N TEXT                adds TEXT to row N's notes, before the row's own
                             "full text: history, row N" marker where it has
                             one, else at their end (notes of `none` are
                             replaced); checks the notes cell and the row's
                             length only, so a failure in another cell does
                             not block it; a row keeps its own cells
  rewrite N FILE             FILE holds row N's whole new line (its # cell N
                             or ?, or the seven cells after it); checks it
                             against the template and writes it in the row's
                             place, its earlier line in the history
                             ("rewritten"): the route that corrects a claim,
                             cuts notes, or moves a reproducer. A FIXED or
                             DUPLICATE row stays so (a FIXED row's commit is
                             checked); a row becomes one only by close or
                             duplicate
  close N --commit HASH --test NAME [--settled TEXT] [--note TEXT] [--claim C]

    @@SC ERR	component trips	acyclic	.../ProjectFortress/demos/trips.fss:98:13-38:     generator extends StandardTotalOrder[\trip\], whose self parameter is trip, but generator is not a subtype of trip.
    @@SC STAGE	component trips	typecheck	errors=18
    @@TC COMPONENT	trips	errors=57

After, on the final `trips.fss`:

    @@SC STAGE	component trips	acyclic	errors=0
    @@SC STAGE	component trips	typecheck	errors=18
    @@TC COMPONENT	trips	errors=54

With the positions masked, the two runs differ in three things only: row 710's message, the two `MIN` and `MAX` declarations that the patch removes (each `errors=0` before), and the component's total.

The driver still refuses the demo:

- 18 typecheck errors:
  - seven `generator` calls whose function it types `ZZ32->List.List[\Any\]`: '(String, ZZ32, ZZ32->List.List[\trip\])->generator is not applicable to an argument of type (String, IntLiteral, ZZ32->List.List[\Any\])' (`:113`, `:130`, `:139`, `:146`, `:153`, `:199`, `:216`);
  - eight `__generate` calls at `Reduction[\List.List[\Any\]\]`;
  - `seq` of a `Range[\ZZ32\]` (`:303`);
  - `perfectSqrt`'s body, typed `AnyMaybe` (`:82`);
  - 'Cannot assign to immutable variable: approx' (`:76`);
- 'Missing parameter type for' `trips`, `xs` and `ps` (`:232`, `:255`, `:263`);
- 'TryChecker returned an untyped expr' at `run`'s comprehension (`:286`);
- in the overloading stage, which the driver runs whatever came before, an `OptionUnwrapException` at `OverloadingChecker.scala:129`.

These are NEW-D-1 (section 12). Walk runs the demo to its end (section 3).

## 5. Where the fix belongs, and the precedent search

- **Generator22D is walk's library**, in `Library/` outside the compiler's files, and no other program imports it. `grep -rln "Generator22D" Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin ProjectFortress/tests ProjectFortress/*_tests ProjectFortress/test_library ProjectFortress/demos explorations --include=*.fs?` lists `Library/Generator22D.fsi`, `Library/Generator22D.fss`, the new test and `ProjectFortress/demos/DemoGenerator22D.fss`. The fix is in its body. Its api (`Library/Generator22D.fsi`) is unchanged.
- **The library halves an integer with `DIV`:**
  - `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4389` (`(self || self)^(n DIV 2)`);
  - `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:364`, `:378`, `:388`, `:396` (`z DIV 2`);
  - `Integral`'s `opr DIV(self,b:I):I` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:461`).

  In `Generator22D.fss` the precedent's defect had three sites. All three are repaired, and no other remains (section 1).
- **The demos' repairs are the probe's**, each in a form that the record or the team's later code uses (the probe's section 6, decision 5). A `ZZ64` or a `QQ` that meets a float goes through `asFloat` (P-74; `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:289`; `nanoTime(): ZZ64`, `:2546`).

  By grep, 16 demos call `nanoTime()`, 42 calls in all, two of them (`trips.fss:238-239`) inside a comment. Each time feeds a repaired line or integer arithmetic: `trips.fss:234`, `turnersParaffins0.fss:436`, and the `DIV` in `ArrayListLong.fss:158` and `PureListLong.fss:152` before their repaired lines. Every one of the 16 reaches its end.
- **`npbft`'s `Complex`** drops `Number`, whose `comprises { RR64, RR32, QQ, AnyIntegral, IntLiteral }` does not list it (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:380-381`). It extends `AdditiveGroup[\Complex\]`, which is `SumReduction`'s bound (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3440`).
- **`trips`'s `MIN` and `MAX`** duplicate `ZZ32`'s own (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:751-752`).
- **Row 710** takes the shape of the demo's own `trip`: `object trip (...) extends StandardTotalOrder[\trip\]` with `opr CMP(self, other:trip)` (`trips.fss:50-54`).
- **The maps place nothing here.** `explorations/coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md` and `modules-and-phases.md` concern phase, checker and walk code, and none of it changes.

## 6. What the specification settles

- `/` on two integers is rational, and `÷` (`DIV`) truncates (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:125-128`). So `rects`'s counts are `DIV`'s.
- A declaration that extends a self-typed trait's instantiation must be a subtype of its self-type argument (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:306-312`). `StandardTotalOrder[\generator\]` meets this rule.
- Nothing in the specification names a demo or `Generator22D`. This rung edits no specification text.

## 7. The stages, the suites and the ladder

- **Neither stage ran.** The rung changes these paths:
  - `Library/Generator22D.fss`;
  - 22 files and the new `GenomeUtil2d.fsi` under `ProjectFortress/demos/`;
  - `ProjectFortress/tests/Generator22DRects.fss`;
  - this folder.

  `Library/Generator22D.fss` and the demos are not among the twelve components that the distance stage reads (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh:85-87`). The count stage reads `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` (`explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh:67`), which imports neither. So neither stage can move.
- **No speed pass.** No checker code changes.
- **No whole suite.** The rung changes no Java or Scala. Its own test ran (section 2), and the gate runs the suites.
- **The ladder subset is empty.** No ladder program's recorded output names anything the rung touched: `grep -rlE "Generator22D|GenomeUtil|demos/|trips|npbft" explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/raw explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/ladder.tsv explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-21/gate/ladder/ladder.tsv` prints nothing (rc 1). The compiled path's library does not hold `Generator22D`.

## 13. Commands worked out

**The demo driver.** It runs from the tree's root, after the setup lines, as `run-demos.sh <out-dir>`:

    set -u
    FH=$PWD ; OUT=$1 ; case "$OUT" in /*) ;; *) OUT="$FH/$OUT" ;; esac ; mkdir -p "$OUT"
    cd "$FH/ProjectFortress/demos"
    LIST=$(ls *.fss | grep -v -E 'Syntax\.fss$|DynamicSemantics\.fss$|Satisfiability\.fss$|GenomeUtil')
    : > "$OUT/summary.tsv"
    for f in $LIST ; do
      n=${f%.fss}
      case "$n" in
        wordcount2) ( cd "$FH" && timeout -k 15 600 bin/fortress ProjectFortress/demos/$f < /dev/null ) > "$OUT/$n.txt" 2>&1 ; rc=$? ;;
        tennisRanking) timeout -k 15 600 ../../bin/fortress $f "$FH/ProjectFortress/demos/tennis050307" "$FH/ProjectFortress/demos/tennis051707" "$FH/ProjectFortress/demos/tennisGames" < /dev/null > "$OUT/$n.txt" 2>&1 ; rc=$? ;;
        *) timeout -k 15 600 ../../bin/fortress $f < /dev/null > "$OUT/$n.txt" 2>&1 ; rc=$? ;;
      esac
      if grep -qi fail "$OUT/$n.txt" ; then fl=fail-in-output ; else fl=clean ; fi
      if [ $rc -eq 0 ] && [ $fl = clean ] ; then v=END ; elif [ $rc -eq 124 ] || [ $rc -eq 137 ] ; then v=LIMIT ; else v=STOP ; fi
      printf '%s\t%s\trc=%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$n" "$v" "$rc" "$fl" "$(grep -v '^ *$' "$OUT/$n.txt" | tail -1 | cut -c1-160)" >> "$OUT/summary.tsv"
    done
    echo "demos: $(grep -c . "$OUT/summary.tsv") run, $(awk -F'\t' '$2=="END"' "$OUT/summary.tsv" | wc -l) reached their end"

**The checker's driver over one demo.** It runs from the tree's root, as steps 1 and 2 of `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh` with the one target:

1. Make `$S/shadow-src` with `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/shadow-patch.py ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress $S/shadow-src && python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/add-patch.py $S/shadow-src`.
2. Compile the seven shadow sources and `DistanceMulti.java`, as `run.sh:102-112` does.
3. Run the driver:

       java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow -Djava.io.tmpdir=$S/tmp -Dfortress.caches=$S/caches \
            -Dprobe.tolerant=true -Dprobe.all=true -Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false \
            -cp $S/shadow-classes:$S/classes:$CP DistanceMulti -order check -setting any ProjectFortress/demos/trips.fss

`CP` is the class path that `run.sh` makes from `bin/fortress_classpath`. The driver's own line reported 53 s for the target before the repair, under `nice -n 19`, nproc 4.

content.content:
7-- A Workflow run starts at most two agents at a time on this machine. The others wait for a free slot. Two agents that build share the four cores.
8-
9:## The disk allowance
10-
11:`df -h /` misleads. Its Size column is the whole disk, about 250 GB, and most of it is reserved and cannot be written. The session may use Used plus Avail, about 37 GB, and Use% is taken of that sum. Read the Avail column: it is what is left.
12-
13:- When the allowance is full, tool output fails with "no space left on device". Check Avail before a long run, and before you seed worktrees or copy builds.
14-- Temporary files that the work never deletes fill it. In this repository, they are mostly the parser's folders in `/tmp`. `fortress-repo`'s `references/build-and-caches.md` gives their sweep.
15-- When it is full, stop your own background processes (`fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md`). Delete what you made and no longer need: scratch, build output, private caches, and finished worktrees whose commits are pushed.
16:- If that is not enough, commit and push, and report that this session's allowance is spent. A new session starts on a fresh machine.
17-
18-## The network
19-
20-Outbound HTTPS goes through the session's proxy, which blocks some hosts. `web.archive.org` resets the connection, and the proxy refuses `labs.oracle.com`.
21-
22-- If you need a research PDF from these hosts, name it in your report. Only the curator can upload it into the session.
23-- To read an archived page that is not a PDF, fetch it through the pure.md reader relay: `https://pure.md/https://web.archive.org/web/<timestamp>if_/<url>`. The `if_` after the timestamp is required.

- F-50 **The compiled checker lets overloads differ in static parameters, as the model of the OOPSLA 2011 paper does, which the specification now states (F-174); as ambiguous, it refuses only the pairs it cannot prove unambiguous.** It builds P-45. It cannot prove a pair over open traits, which no `excludes` or `comprises` clause closes, nor one whose domains exclude only through the exclusion rule and a bound, as the library's `CAP` on `ScalarRange[\I\]` beside `Range2D[\I,J\]` does. It also refuses some pairs that the paper accepts, by its Return Type Rule and by its positional rule, under which two generic declarations in the more-specific relation agree on their static parameters by position (F-75). Other gaps have their own owners: its overloading check never reads a pair of symbolic operators such as `+` (P-155, row 584); two generic arms on a bare type variable fail compiled (F-174, row 537); and walk runs an arm whose size the call leaves unfixed, with the size unbound, where the checker drops the arm or refuses the call (F-69, row 400). Detail: `reviews/overload-static-params-ways.md` sections 2 and 3.

- F-82 **In the interpreter's library, the range types declare a method on the meet for each of their Meet Rule pairs that the compiled checker checks, and their declared types match what their bodies answer.** Among the meets are `CAP` at each rank, a range's number of dimensions (F-89 holds the ranks' kinds), and `FullRange`'s abstract `IN`, so a numeral `IN` a `#` or `:` range type-checks (row 580, fixed). The pairs of `Indexed`'s three subscripts, which the checker skips as operators whose names are symbols (row 584), have no meet in the ranges (F-245). Open library bug (row 603): the full sequential ranges' `map` answers a `SimpleMappedSeqIndexed`, which is no `MappedGenerator`, so its `reverse` is `Indexed`'s. The elements and their order are right, but the string differs: `seq(0:6:2).map(fn x => x + 1).reverse.asString` prints `SimpleReversedIndexed(mapped(seq(1,3,5,7)))`, not `mapped(7,5,3,1)`. `tests/RangeDeclarations.fss` pins that string, and gates the meets. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-range-meets/REPORT.md` section 1.

- F-142 **Walk checks at load the Meet Rule for Functional Methods per providing type.** A type provides what it declares and what it inherits, but not what its `override` declarations override. The check covers every trait, object and object expression. A type with static parameters is checked through one type that stands for all its instances (F-145). That check skips each pair of functional methods whose parameter types mention a static parameter, and each pair that a supertype whose type mentions one provides. Symbolic operators, such as `+` or `||`, are skipped, as the compiled checker skips them. Checked, they would refuse only `EmptyString`'s `||` at load, which one declaration clears (row 611; F-245, measured at `d212b2c1f`). Walk's other refusals at load are in the `fortress-repo` skill's `references/interpreter.md`. Gated by `tests/FunctionalMethodMeet*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-meet/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 7.

content.content:
The rule refuses, rightly, two team declarations, each an open row: the demo `trips.fss`'s `generator` (row 710) and `PureList`'s `List` (row 355). Gated by `compiler_tests/SelfType*` and `XXXSelfType*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-self-type/REPORT.md` sections 1, 2, 4 and 7; `compile-ladder/rung-self-type-exclusion/REPORT.md` section 1.
 only in each leaf leaves the meet refused by the checker's Meet Rule, so `copy` is declared on the meet too (row 467). Its factories are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`. A demo still passes a function to `fill` (row 464). Gated by `tests/TabulateRungA.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-tabulate/REPORT.md` section 2.
- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`; no suite or step of the gate runs them. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the batch that makes the change also rewrites the demo. A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. For example, the change that made `10^(-4)` an error (P-153, the integer power) also wrote `10.0^(-4)` in `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, and `10.0^(-6)` for `10^(-6)` in `npbft.fss`. A demo that fails for want of a feature is made to run again once the feature is built. So the demos known to fail today are to be respelled where the way is known: the five demos that walk refuses at load, since they leave an inherited abstract method without a body (row 670, which names them); `trips.fss`, which walk runs but the compiled checker refuses, since its `generator` object extends `StandardTotalOrder[\trip\]` without being a `trip` (row 710); the timing line of `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, which divides a `ZZ64` by a float and so stops walk (row 791); and the reductions that the compiled checker refuses because they leave out the static argument of a big operator whose bound names its own static parameter, such as `SUM`; their repair writes the argument (row 731).

content.content:
#               target stopped with errors the stage does not count, such as a parse error
#   #kind       by kind (errors.py): exclusion, comprises, overloading, return-type, ...
#   #class      by root cause (classify.py, distance-triage.md section 2), with its name
#   #check      a disagreement: errors.py's and table.py's totals, or sites classify.py cannot
#               find in the tree's library source
#   #unit       by the unit that printed the error first
#   #crash      each declaration, stage or target the checker crashed on
#   #seconds    the run's wall time, and FortressLibrary's, the part that takes it
#   #machine    nproc, CPU model and MHz, load at start, JDK, FORTRESS_THREADS
#   #shadow     whether every shadow edit matched the tracked sources; the last row
# ../distance/compare.sh compares two tables. The run-to-run variation is 2 to 4 errors,
# in the comparisons' and Maybe's pairs and the joins of array bodies (switch-over-
# distance-flat.md section 5).
set -u

OUT=${1:-}
if [ -z "$OUT" ] ; then echo "usage: $0 <out-file> [scratch-dir] [any|walk|compile]" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi
case "$OUT" in /*) ;; *) OUT="$PWD/$OUT" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
D="$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/distance"
SCRATCH=${2:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/distance.$$}
case "$SCRATCH" in /*) ;; *) SCRATCH="$PWD/$SCRATCH" ;; esac
SETTING=${3:-any}
case "$SETTING" in any|walk|compile) ;; *) echo "distance: unknown setting $SETTING" >&2 ; exit 1 ;; esac
FLAGS="-Dprobe.tolerant=true -Dprobe.all=true -Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false"
COMPONENTS="Library/FortressLibrary.fss Library/RangeInternals.fss ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss
 ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss Library/List.fss Library/String.fss Library/FlatString.fss Library/Stream.fss
 ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fss Library/TypeProxy.fss Library/Writer.fss ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss"

rm -rf "$SCRATCH/shadow-src" "$SCRATCH/shadow-classes" "$SCRATCH/classes" "$SCRATCH/caches" "$SCRATCH/tmp"
mkdir -p "$SCRATCH/shadow-src" "$SCRATCH/shadow-classes" "$SCRATCH/classes" "$SCRATCH/caches" "$SCRATCH/tmp" \
         "$(dirname "$OUT")" || exit 1
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1 | sed 's#:[^:]*/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache##')
if [ -z "$CP" ] ; then echo "distance: no classpath from bin/fortress_classpath" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi
MACHINE="nproc=$(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | sed 's/^[^:]*: *//'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | sed 's/^[^:]*: *//') MHz; load at start $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=${FORTRESS_THREADS:-unset}"

# 1. the shadows, from the tracked sources (perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance/make-shadows.sh's
#    steps), and the driver; a text edit that no longer matches is the one way this can go stale
SHADOW="every shadow edit matched the tracked sources"
if ! ( cd "$FH" && python3 "$D/shadow-patch.py" ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress "$SCRATCH/shadow-src" \
                && python3 "$D/add-patch.py" "$SCRATCH/shadow-src" ) > "$SCRATCH/shadows.txt" 2>&1 ; then
    SHADOW="STALE: a shadow edit no longer matches the tracked sources: $(grep -E '^AssertionError' "$SCRATCH/shadows.txt" | tail -1 | tr -s ' ' | cut -c1-200); see $SCRATCH/shadows.txt"
elif ! javac -nowarn -encoding UTF-8 -cp "$CP" -d "$SCRATCH/shadow-classes" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/TypeCheckPhase.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/DesugarPhase.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/CodeGenerationPhase.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/Desugarer.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/nodes_util/NodeComparator.java" >> "$SCRATCH/shadows.txt" 2>&1 ; then
    SHADOW="STALE: the shadow sources no longer compile against the tree; see $SCRATCH/shadows.txt"
elif ! javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d "$SCRATCH/classes" "$D/DistanceMulti.java" >> "$SCRATCH/shadows.txt" 2>&1 ; then
    SHADOW="STALE: DistanceMulti.java no longer compiles against the tree; see $SCRATCH/shadows.txt"
fi

# 2. the run: one JVM, the twelve components, FortressLibrary first so that its run checks
#    the twelve apis with every stage (DistanceMulti.java's header)

## Revival change

**The change.**

- The team's export check (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/ExportChecker.scala` at `a874948ac`) matched a trait's or object's member with any component member of the same header whatever its name (`:600`, the header's name bound to `_`), compared a field by its type alone (`:815`, two statements where one was meant), compared a component's abstract member with the api's with the arguments the wrong way round (`:751`), and asked a matching member for every api member, those written `abstract` included (`:767` and `equalMember`). The tree now matches members by name and header, fields by name, modifiers other than `var` and type, compares the component's abstract members with the api's first, and asks nothing of an api member written `abstract`: tests `XXXExportMemberName`, `XXXExportFieldName`, `ExportVarFieldMatchesField`, `ExportComprisesEllipsisAbstract`, `ExportAbstractMemberDefined`, `ExportAbstractMemberAbsent`. The reason: `Specification/basic/components/apis.tex:252-256`, "A matching definition of a declaration $d$ is a definition $d'$ with the same name as $d$ that includes definitions for all declarations other than the methods or fields declared abstract in $d$. The header and type of $d'$ must be the same as the header and type of $d$."
- The team's interpreter-library api (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` at `a874948ac`) declared without `abstract` members that its component leaves without a body, lacked three bodyless members of the component, declared `EqualTo`'s `opr <(self, other:LessThan)` (line 156) where the component defines it at `GreaterThan`, `ReductionPair[\R,L\] extends SomeReductionPair[\R\]` (line 1749) where the component extends `SomeReductionPair[\L\]`, `Range`'s misspelt `asDebugStriing()` (line 2068) that nothing defines, and `Indexed1` to `Indexed3` without the component's `extends HasRank`. The tree's api writes these as the component has them, with the members that the `abstract` lines need (`ZZ32`'s, `ZZ64`'s and `ZZ`'s, `OpenRange`'s) and `Array2`'s column and row subscripts: shown by the distance stage's export error, 43 entries to 15, and by the walk tests and the model's quick checks, unchanged. The reason: the compiled checker refused the api against its own component (the export error of the stage), and the library's own practice states in the api what the component defines.
- The team's compiler prelude declared `JavaBufferedReader`'s `consume` `throws IOException` in its api (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:600`) and without it in its component (`CompilerBuiltin.fss`, line 1076 at `a874948ac`). The tree's component declares it, as its siblings do: every compiled test compiles the prelude. The reason: the check, comparing names, refused the prelude, 'due to different method consume @ .../CompilerBuiltin.fsi:600:3-601:1'.

**Provenance.** Rows 800, 801 and 802 and the export probe's 4h and 4i (`explorations/perf-probes/export-check-full/REPORT.md`); the batch record's forks 19, 20 and 22 at their defaults, question 2's answer for `BoundedRange`'s `atMost` (P-156), P-27; climb batch 21b, rung E.
## Revival change

### The change

The team's `rectsImpl` counted an array's row and column ranges with `/` (`Library/Generator22D.fss:144-145`, `:150` at a874948ac). In the team's library too, two `ZZ32`s divide to a rational: `ZZ32` extended `ZZ`, whose `opr /(self,other:ZZ):QQ` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:533-534` at a874948ac). So, by reading, `rects` stopped under walk at `array[\Generator[\E\]\](ss0, ss1)` in the team's tree too.

The tree halves with `DIV` (`Library/Generator22D.fss:144`, `:145`, `:150`), and `rects` gives each contiguous rectangle of an `Array2` once. Test: `Generator22DRects`.

Reason: "When the operator / is used to divide one integer by another, the result is rational. The operator ÷ performs truncating integer division" (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:125-128`). The measured failure was 'Failed to find any matching overload, args = (Ratio,Ratio)' at `Library/Generator22D.fss:146`, through the harness on the base.

### Provenance

Row 468, and its stated fix. P-79, the team demos kept running, whose `DemoGenerator22D` needs `rects`. P-27, the library's own practice (`n DIV 2`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4389`). The batch record's fork 23, taken at its default. Climb batch 21b, run 2, rung D.

content.content:
Under walk, the disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses a program's own top-level type that has the name of a type of `FortressLibrary`, such as `Index` or `Indexed`: "Type name may refer to: Index, FortressLibrary.Index". Give such a type another name.

At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function, and checks it as an object. It checks a trait or object with static parameters once, through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a sym

- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the 
  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length, only where one of them has a varargs parameter. Walk checks no other pair of lists of different lengths;
  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations nor a generic one beside a plain one;
  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.

  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with "Cannot find definition for method" (ledger row 780).
  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
